signing_verification.description: Cosign is a container signing, verification, and storage tool from the Sigstore project. It supports keyless signing using OIDC identity providers (GitHub, Google, Microsoft), as well as traditional key-pair signing. Cosign stores signatures as OCI artifacts alongside the signed container image in the same registry, eliminating the need for separate signature storage infrastructure.
signing_verification.use_case: Signing and verifying container images, SBOMs, in-toto attestations, and arbitrary blobs. Primary tool for implementing container supply chain security in CI/CD pipelines.
signing_verification.key_management: Keyless mode: Uses OIDC identity tokens from CI/CD providers (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) to obtain short-lived signing certificates from Fulcio. No long-lived keys to manage. Key-pair mode: Supports KMS-backed keys (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault) and local key pairs.
verification_steps: Pull the signed artifact from the registry
Run cosign verify with the expected identity (--certificate-identity) and OIDC issuer (--certificate-oidc-issuer)
Cosign verifies the signature against the Rekor transparency log
Verify the signing certificate chain back to the Fulcio root CA
Check that the signing identity matches the expected CI/CD workflow
integration_patterns: GitHub Actions: sigstore/cosign-installer action + cosign sign
GitLab CI: cosign sign in .gitlab-ci.yml with OIDC token
Kubernetes: Sigstore Policy Controller or Kyverno admission webhook
Docker: cosign verify before docker pull in deployment scripts

signing_verification.description: Rekor is a transparency log for storing and verifying software supply chain metadata. It provides an immutable, append-only, tamper-evident record of signing events, attestations, and other supply chain metadata. Rekor entries are Merkle tree-backed, enabling efficient inclusion proofs. The public Rekor instance (rekor.sigstore.dev) serves as a shared transparency log for the open source ecosystem.
signing_verification.use_case: Recording and verifying signing events for audit purposes. Detecting equivocation attacks where different consumers receive different signatures for the same artifact. Providing long-term signature verification even after short-lived certificates expire.
signing_verification.key_management: Rekor does not manage signing keys directly. It stores signed entries that reference the signing certificate or public key used. The Rekor server's signing key is used to sign inclusion proofs and tree heads.
verification_steps: Submit the artifact signature and certificate to Rekor for logging
Rekor returns a log entry UUID and signed inclusion proof
Verifiers query Rekor for the log entry by artifact digest or UUID
Verify the inclusion proof against the Rekor tree head
Confirm the signing event timestamp falls within the certificate validity period
integration_patterns: Cosign automatically uploads entries to Rekor during signing
rekor-cli for manual entry submission and verification
Rekor REST API for programmatic integration
Monitor Rekor entries for your organization's artifacts

signing_verification.description: Fulcio is a certificate authority that issues short-lived X.509 signing certificates based on OIDC identity verification. Instead of managing long-lived GPG keys, developers authenticate with their existing identity provider (GitHub, Google, Microsoft), and Fulcio issues a certificate valid for a few minutes -- just long enough to sign an artifact. The certificate embeds the OIDC identity, linking the signature to a verifiable identity.
signing_verification.use_case: Issuing ephemeral signing certificates for keyless code and artifact signing. Eliminating the need for developers to manage GPG keys while maintaining strong identity binding in signatures.
signing_verification.key_management: Fulcio eliminates the need for end-user key management entirely. The signing key is ephemeral, generated client-side for each signing operation, and destroyed after use. The Fulcio root CA certificate anchors the trust chain. Certificate transparency: all issued certificates are logged in a CT log.
verification_steps: Client generates ephemeral key pair
Client authenticates with OIDC provider and receives ID token
Fulcio verifies OIDC token and issues short-lived certificate embedding the OIDC identity
Client uses the ephemeral key to sign the artifact
Certificate and signature are logged in Rekor before the certificate expires
integration_patterns: Cosign handles Fulcio interaction automatically in keyless mode
gitsign uses Fulcio for Git commit signing
CI/CD pipelines use workload identity (OIDC) for automated signing
Custom integrations via Fulcio's REST API

signing_verification.description: The Sigstore Policy Controller is a Kubernetes admission webhook that enforces signature and attestation policies for container images before allowing them to be deployed. It integrates with cosign signatures, Rekor transparency log entries, and in-toto attestations to implement binary authorization at the cluster level. Policies can require specific signers, SLSA provenance levels, or custom attestation predicates.
signing_verification.use_case: Enforcing container image signing policies in Kubernetes clusters. Implementing binary authorization that requires verified provenance before deployment. Blocking unsigned or untrusted container images from running in production.
signing_verification.key_management: Policies reference trusted signing identities (OIDC subjects and issuers) rather than raw public keys. The controller verifies signatures against the Sigstore trust root (Fulcio CA + Rekor) or custom trust roots for enterprise deployments.
verification_steps: Install Policy Controller in the Kubernetes cluster
Define ClusterImagePolicy resources specifying trusted signing identities
When a pod is created, the admission webhook intercepts the request
Controller verifies that all container images have valid signatures from trusted identities
Pod creation is allowed only if all image policies are satisfied
integration_patterns: Kubernetes ClusterImagePolicy CRD for policy definition
Namespace-level enforcement with label-based opt-in/opt-out
Integration with cosign signatures and in-toto attestations
Combined with OPA/Gatekeeper for comprehensive admission control

signing_verification.description: Gitsign is a Sigstore project that enables keyless Git commit and tag signing using Sigstore's infrastructure (Fulcio certificates, Rekor transparency log). Instead of managing GPG keys or SSH signing keys, developers authenticate with their OIDC identity provider to sign commits. This dramatically simplifies the adoption of commit signing by eliminating key generation, distribution, and rotation overhead.
signing_verification.use_case: Signing Git commits and tags without managing GPG keys. Verifying developer identity on commits through OIDC identity providers. Implementing commit signing in organizations where GPG key management is impractical.
signing_verification.key_management: No key management required. Each commit signing event uses a new ephemeral key pair and a Fulcio certificate bound to the developer's OIDC identity. The signature and certificate are recorded in Rekor for long-term verification.
verification_steps: Developer configures Git to use gitsign as the signing program
On git commit -S, gitsign initiates OIDC authentication
Fulcio issues a short-lived certificate with the developer's identity
Commit is signed with the ephemeral key
Signature and certificate are logged in Rekor
Verification: gitsign verify checks Rekor log for the signing event
integration_patterns: Git config: gpg.format = x509, gpg.x509.program = gitsign
GitHub: verified commit badges via Sigstore trust root
CI/CD: verify commit signatures in pipeline using gitsign-credential-cache
Enterprise: custom Fulcio instance for internal OIDC providers

signing_verification.description: Cosign supports creating and verifying in-toto attestations attached to container images. Attestations allow producers to make verifiable claims about their artifacts, such as SLSA provenance, vulnerability scan results, SBOM data, and compliance status. Attestations are stored as OCI artifacts alongside the container image and can be verified using cosign verify-attestation.
signing_verification.use_case: Attaching verifiable metadata (SLSA provenance, SBOM, scan results) to container images. Enabling policy-based verification of artifact properties beyond just signing identity. Supporting multi-layer trust decisions based on build provenance, security scans, and compliance attestations.
signing_verification.key_management: Same as cosign signing: keyless via Fulcio/OIDC or KMS-backed keys. The attestation is signed with the same mechanisms used for image signing.
verification_steps: Create an in-toto attestation using cosign attest with a predicate file
Cosign signs the attestation and attaches it to the image in the registry
Verifier runs cosign verify-attestation with the expected predicate type
Optionally apply CUE or Rego policies to validate attestation contents
Admission controllers can enforce attestation requirements at deployment
integration_patterns: SLSA provenance: cosign attest with SLSA predicate type
SBOM: cosign attach sbom or cosign attest with CycloneDX/SPDX predicate
Vulnerability scans: cosign attest with vuln predicate type
Policy enforcement: Kyverno or Sigstore Policy Controller verify attestations

signing_verification.description: The SLSA Verifier is a tool for verifying SLSA provenance of artifacts produced by trusted builders. It validates that the provenance was generated by a known builder (e.g., slsa-github-generator), that the provenance is correctly signed, and that it matches the artifact being verified. The verifier supports npm packages, container images, and generic artifacts.
signing_verification.use_case: Verifying SLSA provenance of software artifacts before consumption or deployment. Implementing supply chain verification in CI/CD pipelines or deployment processes. Validating that artifacts were built by trusted build platforms.
signing_verification.key_management: The verifier uses embedded trust roots for known SLSA builders (GitHub Actions builders). For custom builders, the verifier can be configured with custom trust roots. No key management is required by the consumer.
verification_steps: Download the artifact and its provenance attestation
Run slsa-verifier verify-artifact with the artifact, provenance, and expected source repository
Verifier checks: provenance signature validity, builder identity, source repository match, build trigger
Verifier outputs the verified build details including source commit and builder identity
Consumer can optionally verify additional provenance fields (branch, tag, workflow)
integration_patterns: CI/CD: slsa-verifier verify-artifact in dependency verification steps
npm: slsa-verifier verify-npm-package for npm packages with SLSA provenance
Container: cosign verify-attestation with SLSA predicate type
Policy: integrate with admission controllers for deployment verification

signing_verification.description: In-toto layouts define the expected steps and inspections in a software supply chain. A layout is signed by a project owner and specifies which functionaries (people or systems) are authorized to perform each step, what materials (inputs) and products (outputs) each step should have, and what inspections should be performed on the final product. Layouts are the policy language of in-toto.
signing_verification.use_case: Defining and enforcing end-to-end supply chain policies. Specifying who is authorized to perform each step in the build/release process. Detecting unauthorized modifications to the supply chain process.
signing_verification.key_management: Project owners sign layouts with their private keys. Layout keys must be securely distributed to verifiers. Functionary keys are referenced in the layout to identify authorized step performers. Supports key rotation through layout updates.
verification_steps: Project owner creates a layout defining expected supply chain steps
Each functionary performs their step and generates a signed link metadata file

At verification time, the verifier checks: layout signature validity, all required steps have link metadata, link metadata signatures match authorized functionaries, material/product rules are satisfied across steps
integration_patterns: CI/CD: in-toto-run wraps each build step to generate link metadata
Release: in-toto-verify validates all links against the layout before release
Policy updates: new layouts are signed and distributed when the supply chain changes
Integration with SLSA: in-toto attestation format is the basis for SLSA provenance

signing_verification.description: Link metadata is generated by each functionary (step performer) in an in-toto supply chain. Each link records the materials (inputs) consumed and products (outputs) produced by the step, along with the command executed and any byproducts. Links are cryptographically signed by the functionary's key, providing non-repudiable evidence of who performed each step and what was processed.
signing_verification.use_case: Recording evidence of each supply chain step execution. Providing a verifiable record of build inputs and outputs. Enabling end-to-end supply chain verification by chaining links together.
signing_verification.key_management: Each functionary has a signing key used to sign their link metadata. Keys can be GPG, RSA, or Ed25519. For automated steps (CI/CD), the signing key is typically stored in a secure vault or KMS. The layout references the expected public keys for each step.
verification_steps: Functionary runs in-toto-run to execute a step and generate link metadata
in-toto-run records: step name, command, materials (hashes of inputs), products (hashes of outputs), return code
Link metadata is signed with the functionary's private key
Verifier collects all link metadata and the layout
in-toto-verify checks that links satisfy all layout rules
integration_patterns: Build step: in-toto-run --step-name compile -- make build
Test step: in-toto-run --step-name test -- make test
Package step: in-toto-run --step-name package -- npm pack
Automated: in-toto-run with KMS-backed signing in CI/CD pipelines

signing_verification.description: The in-toto Attestation Framework defines a standardized format for signed attestations about software artifacts. An attestation consists of an envelope (containing the signature) and a statement (containing the subject artifacts and a predicate with the attestation content). The framework is used as the basis for SLSA provenance, CycloneDX attestations, and custom attestation types.
signing_verification.use_case: Standardized format for expressing verifiable claims about software artifacts. Foundation for SLSA provenance attestations. Enabling interoperability between different supply chain security tools through a common attestation format.
signing_verification.key_management: Attestations are wrapped in DSSE (Dead Simple Signing Envelope) which supports multiple signature formats. Signing can use any key type: GPG, PKCS#1, Ed25519, or Sigstore keyless (Fulcio certificates).
verification_steps: Verify the DSSE envelope signature
Extract the statement from the envelope
Verify that the statement subject matches the artifact being verified (by digest)
Parse the predicate according to its predicate type
Apply predicate-specific verification rules (e.g., SLSA provenance verification)
integration_patterns: SLSA: slsa-github-generator produces in-toto attestations with SLSA Provenance predicate
Cosign: cosign attest creates in-toto attestations attached to container images
Custom: create custom predicate types for organization-specific attestations
Verification: cosign verify-attestation or in-toto-verify for attestation checking

signing_verification.description: Inspections are verification-time operations defined in an in-toto layout that run commands and check their results against expected values. Unlike steps (which are performed by functionaries during the supply chain), inspections run at verification time to perform additional checks such as verifying that packages match their expected checksums, running linters on the final product, or checking that no unauthorized files are present.
signing_verification.use_case: Performing verification-time checks on the final artifact. Validating properties that can only be checked after all supply chain steps are complete. Adding consumer-side verification logic beyond simple signature checking.
signing_verification.key_management: Inspections do not require separate key management as they run at verification time. The inspection definitions are part of the signed layout, so they are protected by the layout owner's signature.
verification_steps: Layout defines inspections with commands and expected output patterns
During in-toto-verify, each inspection is executed
Inspection output (materials and products) is checked against layout rules
If any inspection fails, the entire verification fails
Inspections can cross-reference link metadata from previous steps
integration_patterns: Checksum verification: inspect that final artifact matches expected hash
License compliance: inspect that no disallowed licenses appear in the BOM
File integrity: inspect that the release contains only expected files
SBOM validation: inspect that the SBOM matches the actual package contents

signing_verification.description: Notary v2, implemented as the 'notation' CLI tool, is a CNCF project for signing and verifying OCI artifacts (container images, Helm charts, etc.). It uses the OCI distribution specification's referrers API to store signatures as OCI artifacts linked to the signed image. Notation supports pluggable trust policies and signing key providers, making it suitable for enterprise environments with existing PKI infrastructure.
signing_verification.use_case: Enterprise container image signing with organizational PKI. Signing OCI artifacts in registries that support the OCI 1.1 referrers API. Implementing container supply chain security with custom trust policies and key management.
signing_verification.key_management: Supports pluggable key providers: AWS Signer, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault, local key pairs. Enterprise-friendly: integrates with existing corporate PKI and certificate management infrastructure. Certificates follow X.509 standards with configurable trust stores and trust policies.
verification_steps: Configure trust policy defining trusted registries and signing identities
Run notation verify against the signed OCI artifact
Notation retrieves signatures from the registry using the referrers API
Verifies signature against the trust policy (trusted certificates, revocation check)
Returns verification result including the signing identity and timestamp
integration_patterns: Azure: notation sign with Azure Key Vault plugin
AWS: notation sign with AWS Signer plugin
Kubernetes: Ratify admission controller for runtime verification
CI/CD: notation sign in build pipeline, notation verify before deployment

signing_verification.description: ORAS enables pushing and pulling any type of content to and from OCI-compliant registries, not just container images. This is the foundation for storing supply chain metadata (signatures, SBOMs, attestations, provenance) alongside container images in the same registry. ORAS implements the OCI distribution specification's referrers API for linking artifacts to their parent images.
signing_verification.use_case: Storing and retrieving supply chain artifacts (SBOMs, signatures, attestations) in OCI registries. Attaching metadata to container images using the OCI referrers API. Building supply chain tooling that leverages existing container registry infrastructure.
signing_verification.key_management: ORAS itself does not handle signing or key management. It provides the storage layer for signed artifacts. Signing is handled by tools like cosign or notation that store their output using OCI-compatible storage (which ORAS implements).
verification_steps: Push artifacts to OCI registry: oras push registry.example.com/repo:tag file.json
Attach artifact to parent image: oras attach with --artifact-type
Discover attached artifacts: oras discover to list referrers
Pull attached artifacts: oras pull to retrieve attached SBOMs, signatures, etc.
integration_patterns: SBOM attachment: oras attach --artifact-type 'application/spdx+json' sbom.json
Signature storage: cosign and notation use OCI referrers API internally
CI/CD: oras push to store build metadata alongside images
Discovery: oras discover to find all metadata attached to an image

signing_verification.description: Ratify is a Kubernetes admission controller that verifies supply chain metadata (signatures, SBOMs, attestations) for container images before allowing deployment. It integrates with Notary v2 (notation), cosign, and other verification plugins. Ratify is designed for enterprise Kubernetes environments and supports complex verification policies including certificate chain validation and custom plugin extensions.
signing_verification.use_case: Kubernetes admission control for container supply chain verification. Enforcing organizational policies requiring signed images, valid SBOMs, or specific attestations before deployment. Enterprise alternative to Sigstore Policy Controller with broader plugin support.
signing_verification.key_management: Ratify delegates key management to verification plugins (notation, cosign). Trust policies are configured as Kubernetes CRDs. Certificate stores can reference Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or inline certificates.
verification_steps: Deploy Ratify as a Kubernetes admission controller
Configure verification policies using CRDs (Store, Verifier, Policy)
When a pod creation request arrives, Ratify intercepts it
For each container image, Ratify discovers and verifies attached signatures and attestations
Pod creation is allowed only if all verification policies pass
integration_patterns: Notation verifier: verify notation signatures using Notary v2
Cosign verifier: verify cosign keyless signatures
SBOM verifier: verify that a valid SBOM is attached
Custom plugins: write custom verifiers for organization-specific requirements

signing_verification.description: GPG (GNU Privacy Guard) is the traditional method for signing Git commits and tags using asymmetric cryptography. Each developer generates a GPG key pair, registers the public key with their Git hosting platform (GitHub, GitLab), and configures Git to sign commits with their private key. GPG signing provides strong identity verification but requires manual key management, distribution, and rotation.
signing_verification.use_case: Verifying developer identity on Git commits. Meeting compliance requirements for non-repudiation in code changes. Establishing a trust chain from developer identity to committed code.
signing_verification.key_management: Manual key management: developers generate key pairs, upload public keys to keyservers and Git platforms, and protect private keys on their workstations. Key rotation requires re-uploading new keys. Key revocation requires publishing revocation certificates. Enterprise: can use smart cards (YubiKey) for hardware-backed key storage.
verification_steps: Developer generates GPG key pair: gpg --full-generate-key
Public key uploaded to Git platform (GitHub/GitLab settings)
Git configured: git config --global commit.gpgsign true
Commits are signed: git commit -S -m 'message'
Verification: git log --show-signature or GitHub 'Verified' badge
integration_patterns: GitHub: upload GPG public key to account settings, commits show 'Verified' badge
GitLab: upload GPG key, configure push rules to require signed commits
CI/CD: verify commit signatures in pipeline before building
YubiKey: store GPG signing subkey on hardware token for enhanced security

signing_verification.description: Git 2.34+ supports commit and tag signing using SSH keys, providing a simpler alternative to GPG signing. Developers can reuse their existing SSH keys for commit signing, eliminating the need for separate GPG key management. GitHub and GitLab both support SSH commit signature verification, displaying 'Verified' badges for commits signed with registered SSH keys.
signing_verification.use_case: Simplified commit signing using existing SSH key infrastructure. Lower barrier to adoption compared to GPG signing. Useful for organizations where developers already have SSH keys but lack GPG setup.
signing_verification.key_management: Uses existing SSH keys (Ed25519 or RSA). Keys are typically already managed for Git access. Allowed signers file maps SSH keys to email identities. No keyservers required -- public keys are registered directly with Git platforms. Hardware-backed keys supported via FIDO2/YubiKey.
verification_steps: Configure Git: git config --global gpg.format ssh
Set signing key: git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
Create allowed signers file mapping keys to identities
Configure: git config --global gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile ~/.ssh/allowed_signers
Verify: git log --show-signature
integration_patterns: GitHub: upload SSH signing key (separate from authentication key)
GitLab: SSH signing keys in user settings
Automation: SSH keys stored in CI/CD secrets for automated signing
FIDO2: YubiKey with resident SSH key for hardware-backed signing

signing_verification.description: GPG signing is the traditional method for signing software packages in Linux distributions (RPM, DEB), Python packages, and other distribution systems. The package maintainer signs the package with their GPG private key, and consumers verify the signature using the maintainer's public key. This model has been the backbone of Linux distribution security for decades.
signing_verification.use_case: Signing Linux distribution packages (RPM, DEB). Signing Python packages for PyPI. Signing release artifacts (tarballs, binaries) for open source projects. Traditional package integrity verification.
signing_verification.key_management: Project or distribution maintainers manage long-lived GPG keys. Public keys distributed through keyservers, project websites, or package repositories (apt-key, rpm --import). Key rotation requires trust delegation and transition periods. Some distributions use a hierarchical key model with signing sub-keys.
verification_steps: Import the project's GPG public key
Download the package and its detached signature (.asc or .sig file)
Verify: gpg --verify package.tar.gz.asc package.tar.gz
For RPM: rpm --checksig package.rpm
For APT: apt-key and repository signing verification
integration_patterns: RPM: rpmsign --addsign for RPM package signing
DEB: dpkg-sig or debsign for Debian package signing
PyPI: GPG signatures (deprecated in favor of PEP 740 attestations)
Generic: gpg --detach-sign -a for any file

signing_verification.description: TUF is a security framework for software update systems that protects against various attacks on update infrastructure. It uses a hierarchy of signed metadata (root, targets, snapshot, timestamp) with role-based key management and delegated trust. TUF is designed to be resilient against key compromise, rollback attacks, mix-and-match attacks, and freeze attacks. It is the foundation for package security in PyPI, Homebrew, and other ecosystems.
signing_verification.use_case: Securing software update and distribution systems against infrastructure-level attacks. Providing rollback protection, ensuring update freshness, and managing key compromise recovery. Foundation for package registry security (PyPI, Homebrew, Docker Content Trust).
signing_verification.key_management: Hierarchical key roles: root (offline, highest trust), targets (signs package metadata), snapshot (signs collection of targets), timestamp (signs freshness). Threshold signing: multiple keys required for critical roles. Key rotation built into the framework. Supports offline keys for root role.
verification_steps: Client fetches the latest timestamp metadata (freshness check)
Verifies snapshot metadata consistency
Fetches targets metadata for the desired package
Verifies package digest matches targets metadata
Downloads package and verifies integrity
Rollback protection: client rejects metadata with version numbers lower than previously seen
integration_patterns: PyPI: PEP 458 implements TUF for PyPI package distribution
Docker: Docker Content Trust (DCT) is based on TUF via Notary v1
Homebrew: uses TUF for formula verification
Custom: python-tuf library for building TUF-protected update systems

signing_verification.description: TUF's root rotation mechanism enables recovery from root key compromise without requiring a new trust anchor. The root metadata is self-signed and includes its own version number, the current set of trusted root keys, and the threshold number of signatures required. When root keys need to be rotated, a new root metadata file is signed by both the old and new root keys, creating a verified transition.
signing_verification.use_case: Recovering from root key compromise in update systems. Planned rotation of root signing keys. Adding or removing root key holders when organizational responsibilities change.
signing_verification.key_management: Root keys are stored offline (air-gapped systems, hardware tokens). Threshold signing requires multiple root key holders to authorize changes. New root metadata must be signed by both the previous threshold of keys and the new set of keys, ensuring continuity of trust.
verification_steps: New root metadata is created with updated key set and incremented version
New root metadata is signed by the threshold of existing root keys AND the new root keys
Client fetches the new root metadata
Client verifies the new root using the previous root's keys (chain of trust)
Client updates its trusted root to the new version
Process repeats for each root version to reach the latest
integration_patterns: Ceremony: offline key signing ceremony with multiple key holders
python-tuf: programmatic root rotation via TUF library
go-tuf: Go implementation supporting root rotation
Repository tools: tuf-on-ci for automated TUF metadata management

signing_verification.description: TUF supports delegated targets, where the authority to sign for specific packages or paths is delegated from the top-level targets role to other signing roles. This enables scalable trust management where different teams or individuals can sign for their specific packages without requiring access to the top-level targets key. Delegations can be nested, creating a hierarchy of trust.
signing_verification.use_case: Scaling package signing across large organizations with many packages. Enabling individual package maintainers to sign their own packages within a trusted framework. Implementing trust delegation for community package repositories.
signing_verification.key_management: The top-level targets role delegates to sub-roles by specifying the delegated paths (packages), the delegated keys, and the signature threshold. Delegated roles manage their own keys independently. Delegations can be further nested for fine-grained access control.
verification_steps: Client resolves which delegation is responsible for the requested package
Follows the delegation chain from targets to the responsible delegated role
Verifies each delegation signature in the chain
Verifies the final delegated targets metadata for the specific package
Downloads and verifies the package against the signed metadata
integration_patterns: PyPI: PEP 480 proposed delegated signing for individual package maintainers
Repository management: delegate signing authority by team or package namespace
Enterprise: delegate signing by department or product team
Community: allow individual maintainers to sign without top-level key access

signing_verification.description: npm provenance enables packages published from supported CI/CD systems (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) to include a cryptographically signed SLSA provenance attestation. The attestation links the published package to its source repository, build workflow, and commit, enabling consumers to verify that a package was built from its claimed source. Provenance uses Sigstore for keyless signing.
signing_verification.use_case: Verifying that npm packages were built from their claimed source repository by a trusted CI/CD system. Detecting supply chain attacks where package contents do not match the source code. Building trust in the npm ecosystem through verifiable provenance.
signing_verification.key_management: Keyless signing via Sigstore: the CI/CD OIDC token authenticates the build to Fulcio, which issues a short-lived certificate. No key management required by package publishers. Signatures are verified against the Sigstore trust root.
verification_steps: Publisher: npm publish --provenance in a supported CI/CD environment
npm generates SLSA Provenance v1 attestation signed with Sigstore
Attestation is stored in npm's attestation storage
Consumer: npm audit signatures verifies all installed packages
Consumers can also check provenance on npmjs.com package pages
integration_patterns: GitHub Actions: npm publish --provenance (OIDC token provided automatically)
GitLab CI: npm publish --provenance with OIDC configuration
Verification: npm audit signatures in CI/CD or developer workflows
Policy: require provenance for all production dependencies

signing_verification.description: The npm audit signatures command verifies the registry signatures and provenance attestations of all installed packages. Registry signatures verify that the package was signed by the npm registry, while provenance attestations verify that the package was built from its claimed source. This provides a comprehensive supply chain verification check for npm dependency trees.
signing_verification.use_case: Verifying integrity and provenance of all installed npm packages. Detecting tampered packages in the dependency tree. Implementing supply chain verification as part of CI/CD pipelines or security audits.
signing_verification.key_management: No key management required by consumers. The npm registry's signing key and the Sigstore trust root are embedded in the npm CLI. Verification is fully automated.
verification_steps: Run npm audit signatures in the project directory
npm checks registry signatures for all installed packages
npm checks provenance attestations where available
Report shows: verified (good), missing signature (warning), invalid signature (error)
CI/CD: fail the build if any package has an invalid signature
integration_patterns: CI/CD: npm audit signatures as a build step
Pre-deploy: verify signatures before deployment
Monitoring: periodic signature audits of production dependencies
Policy: require all dependencies to have valid signatures

signing_verification.description: PEP 740 introduces attestation support for PyPI, enabling package publishers to attach cryptographically signed attestations to their packages. Attestations use the in-toto attestation format with Sigstore signing, providing verifiable claims about package provenance. The Trusted Publisher mechanism links PyPI packages to their source repositories through OIDC, enabling keyless signing from CI/CD.
signing_verification.use_case: Verifying that PyPI packages were built from their claimed source repository. Attaching verifiable metadata (provenance, SBOM, vulnerability scans) to Python packages. Building trust in the PyPI ecosystem through cryptographic attestations.
signing_verification.key_management: Keyless via Sigstore Trusted Publishers. Package publishers configure a Trusted Publisher relationship linking their PyPI project to a GitHub/GitLab repository. OIDC tokens from CI/CD authenticate the publisher to Sigstore for signing. No manual key management required.
verification_steps: Publisher configures Trusted Publisher on PyPI for their project
CI/CD workflow uses pypi-attestation or twine to publish with attestations
Sigstore signs the attestation with a certificate linked to the CI/CD identity
Consumer: pip install with attestation verification (when available)
Programmatic: pypi-attestation verify for manual verification
integration_patterns: GitHub Actions: pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish with attestations enabled
Trusted Publisher: OIDC federation between GitHub/GitLab and PyPI
Verification: pypi-attestation CLI tool for verifying attestations
Policy: require attestations for critical Python dependencies

signing_verification.description: PyPI Trusted Publishers is an OIDC-based authentication mechanism that replaces API tokens for package publishing. Instead of storing a long-lived PyPI API token in CI/CD secrets, publishers configure a trust relationship between their PyPI project and their CI/CD platform (GitHub, GitLab). The CI/CD OIDC token is used directly for authentication, eliminating the risk of token theft and enabling provenance-linked publishing.
signing_verification.use_case: Secure, tokenless package publishing to PyPI from CI/CD pipelines. Eliminating the risk of API token theft for PyPI publishing. Enabling provenance attestations by linking packages to their CI/CD source.
signing_verification.key_management: No API tokens or keys to manage. The trust relationship is configured in PyPI's web interface by specifying the authorized GitHub/GitLab repository, workflow, and environment. OIDC tokens are short-lived and scoped to the specific CI/CD job.
verification_steps: Configure Trusted Publisher on PyPI: specify repository, workflow, and optional environment
In CI/CD: use pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish which handles OIDC exchange automatically
PyPI verifies the OIDC token against the configured trust relationship
If valid, PyPI issues a short-lived publishing token
Package is published with the CI/CD identity linked to the publication event
integration_patterns: GitHub Actions: pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish with id-token: write permission
GitLab CI: PyPI Trusted Publisher with GitLab OIDC
Migration: replace stored API tokens with Trusted Publisher configuration
Combined: Trusted Publishers + attestations for full provenance chain

signing_verification.description: Docker Content Trust uses The Update Framework (TUF) via Notary v1 to sign and verify Docker container images. When DCT is enabled, Docker clients only pull images that have been signed by trusted publishers. DCT provides integrity verification, publisher identity verification, and freshness guarantees through TUF's timestamp mechanism. While functional, DCT is being superseded by cosign and Notary v2 for new deployments.
signing_verification.use_case: Signing and verifying Docker container images using TUF-based trust. Enforcing image signing policies in Docker environments. Legacy container signing for environments that use Notary v1 infrastructure.
signing_verification.key_management: Root key: generated offline during first push (should be stored securely, e.g., YubiKey). Repository key: generated per-repository, used for day-to-day signing. Timestamp key: managed by the Notary server. Delegation keys: allow delegating signing authority to specific users or CI/CD systems.
verification_steps: Enable DCT: export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
On docker push, images are signed with the repository key
Signatures are stored on the Notary server
On docker pull, the client verifies TUF metadata chain
Pull fails if no valid signature exists or if TUF metadata has expired
integration_patterns: Enable globally: DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 in environment
CI/CD: sign images during build, verify before deployment
Delegation: delegate signing to CI/CD keys while root key stays offline
Migration: consider migrating to cosign or Notary v2 for new projects
signing_verification.keywords: docker content trust,dct,notary v1,tuf,container signing,legacy,image trust

signing_verification.description: Docker Scout generates and attaches SBOM attestations to container images, providing a verifiable inventory of all packages and libraries within the image. The SBOM is created by analyzing the image layers and stored as an in-toto attestation using the SPDX predicate type. Docker Scout SBOMs enable vulnerability scanning, license compliance checking, and supply chain transparency for containerized applications.
signing_verification.use_case: Generating and attaching SBOMs to Docker container images. Enabling vulnerability scanning based on accurate package inventories. Meeting regulatory requirements (EU CRA) for SBOM provision in containerized products.
signing_verification.key_management: SBOM attestations can be signed using cosign (keyless via Sigstore) or Docker's built-in attestation mechanisms. Docker Buildx supports creating provenance and SBOM attestations during the build process using the --sbom flag.
verification_steps: Build with SBOM: docker buildx build --sbom=true
SBOM attestation is attached to the image as an OCI artifact
Verify: docker scout cves to scan the SBOM for vulnerabilities
Inspect: docker scout sbom to view the SBOM contents
Export: docker scout sbom --format spdx-json for external tools
integration_patterns: Build: docker buildx build --sbom=true --provenance=true
CI/CD: generate SBOM during image build, scan before push
Registry: SBOM attestations stored alongside image in registry
Compliance: export SBOM in SPDX or CycloneDX format for regulatory reporting

signing_verification.description: Docker Buildx can generate SLSA provenance attestations during the image build process. The provenance records the builder identity, source repository, build configuration, and materials used during the build. Provenance attestations are attached to the image as OCI artifacts and can be verified using cosign or slsa-verifier. This provides SLSA Level 1-2 compliance for Docker image builds.
signing_verification.use_case: Generating SLSA provenance for Docker container images during the build process. Meeting SLSA requirements for container-based software. Providing verifiable build origin information to image consumers.
signing_verification.key_management: Provenance attestations are signed by the build system. When building with Docker Buildx on GitHub Actions, the OIDC token can be used for Sigstore keyless signing. The provenance signature links the build to the CI/CD identity.
verification_steps: Build with provenance: docker buildx build --provenance=true
Provenance attestation is attached to the image
Inspect: docker buildx imagetools inspect to view attestations
Verify: cosign verify-attestation with SLSA predicate type
Verify source: check that source repository and commit match expectations
integration_patterns: GitHub Actions: docker/build-push-action with provenance: true
GitLab CI: docker buildx build --provenance=true in .gitlab-ci.yml
Verification: cosign verify-attestation in deployment pipeline
Policy: require SLSA provenance for all production container images
